newsitem.title: GERMANY: Commerzbank sees evasion probe ending soon.
newsitem.headline: Commerzbank sees evasion probe ending soon.

text.p: Germany's Commerzbank AG said on Tuesday it expected a swift resolution to a 14-month old probe into alleged corporate tax evasion by senior executives, including its chairman Martin Kohlhaussen.

The probe follows a raid on the bank's premises in February 1996, after which the bank was forced to repay several hundred million marks in back-tax for the period from 1984 to 1995. The investigation widened to include Kohlhaussen last September.
"The investigations have not yet been fully completed but we are confident they will reach a successful resolution," Kohlhaussen told reporters at the company's annual results conference.

Commerzbank has stressed that Kohlhaussen's involvement in the case stems from the fact that he signed tax returns during the period in dispute and does not amount to suspicion of personal tax evasion.

The Commerzbank chairman, a high-profile banker who has consistently complained of over-aggressive raids by tax investigators on bank premises and records, said the incident would not weigh on 1997 earnings.
The bank had made more than adequate provision for any potential losses, he said. Talks with investigators had been proceeding "satisfactorily".
Commerzbank has been disputing the size of the tax repayment and has said in the past it paid out 5.2 billion marks ($3 billion) in taxes during the period.

Prosecutors have said they are looking into the valuation of items on Commerzbank's balance sheet, particularly losses booked at group level for U.S. subsidiaries which they claim had already been written off in the U.S.
